ALU: Arithmetic Logic Unit: the part of the CPU that does calculations and logic.
AND: Logic gate: the output is true only if both inputs are true.
ASCII: A character set that gives basic English characters a number, using 7-8 bits.
BIOS: Basic Input/Output System: start-up instructions stored in ROM.
CPU: Central Processing Unit: the part of the computer that runs instructions.
CSV: Comma Separated Values: a text file where each line is a row and commas split the values.
DELETE: SQL command that removes rows matching a condition.
FTP: File Transfer Protocol: the rules for sending files between computers.
GDPR: General Data Protection Regulation: laws on how personal data must be handled.
UK GDPR: The UK's version of GDPR: laws on how personal data must be handled.
HDD: Hard Disk Drive: magnetic storage on spinning platters. Cheap and large, but slower.
HTTP: HyperText Transfer Protocol: the rules for sending web pages.
HTTPS: HTTP with encryption, so data can't be read on its way across the network.
IDE: Integrated Development Environment: a code editor, translator and debugger in one program.
IMAP: Internet Message Access Protocol: reads email from a server and leaves it there.
INSERT: SQL command that adds a new row to a table.
IP: Internet Protocol: gives packets an address and routes them across networks.
LAN: Local Area Network: a network covering a small area, like one building.
NIC: Network Interface Card: the hardware that connects a device to a network.
NOT: Logic gate: flips its input, so true becomes false and false becomes true.
OR: Logic gate: the output is true if at least one input is true.
OS: Operating System: software that manages the computer's hardware and runs programs.
POP3: Post Office Protocol 3: downloads email to your device.
RAM: Random Access Memory: fast, temporary memory for running programs and data.
ROM: Read Only Memory: permanent memory holding the instructions needed to start up.
SELECT: SQL command that retrieves data from a table.
SMTP: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol: sends email to and between mail servers.
SQL: Structured Query Language: the language used to work with databases.
SSD: Solid State Drive: storage with no moving parts. Fast and quiet, but costs more per gigabyte.
TCP: Transmission Control Protocol: sets up the connection and splits data into packets.
UPDATE: SQL command that changes existing rows matching a condition.
WAN: Wide Area Network: a network covering a large area, often using third-party links.
WHERE: SQL clause that filters which rows are returned.
Computer Misuse Act: UK law that makes unauthorised access to computers or data illegal.
Data Protection Act: UK law that sets rules for how personal data is collected, used and kept.
Ethernet: The standard way of connecting devices with cables in a wired network.
von Neumann: A design where instructions and data are stored together in main memory.
abstraction: Removing unnecessary detail so you can focus on what matters.
access control: Limiting who can see or change things, using accounts, passwords and access levels.
acceptable use policy: Rules on how a system may be used.
algorithmic bias: Unfair results from a computer system, often caused by biased training data.
anti-malware: Software that finds and removes malicious software.
audit trail: A record of who did what, and when.
authentication: Confirming who a user is, for example with an ID and password.
bandwidth: How much data can be sent per second.
bitmap: An image stored as a grid of pixels.
bit depth: The number of bits used for each sound sample.
boundary: Boundary data: test values right at the edge of what is allowed.
brute-force: Trying lots of passwords automatically until one works.
brute force: Trying lots of passwords automatically until one works.
bus: Wires that carry data and signals between components. In a network, one shared main cable.
cache: Small, very fast memory that holds frequently used data close to the CPU.
clock speed: How many cycles the CPU runs per second, which sets how many instructions it can do.
code review: Other people checking the code for mistakes and security holes.
colour depth: The number of bits per pixel. More bits means more possible colours.
compiler: Translates the whole program into machine code before it runs.
control unit: The part of the CPU that directs the fetch-decode-execute cycle.
copyright: Automatic legal protection for original work, such as code.
decomposition: Breaking a big problem into smaller, manageable parts.
denial-of-service: An attack that overwhelms a service with traffic so people can't use it.
digital exclusion: People being left behind because they have no access to devices or the internet.
driver: Software that lets the operating system control a piece of hardware.
e-waste: Discarded electronic devices, which can contain harmful materials.
encryption: Scrambling data so it can't be read without the key.
erroneous: Erroneous data: invalid input that should be rejected safely.
ethical hacking: Hacking done with permission to find weaknesses so they can be fixed.
firewall: Filters network traffic and blocks anything unauthorised.
foreign key: A field that links a row to the primary key of another table.
function: A subprogram that returns a value.
identifier: The name of a variable or subprogram.
interpreter: Translates and runs a program one line at a time.
iteration: Repeating statements, using loops such as for and while.
lossless: Compression that lets the original be rebuilt perfectly.
lossy: Compression that permanently throws away some data to save space.
machine code: The binary instructions a CPU can run directly.
malware: Software designed to cause harm, such as viruses, worms, Trojans and ransomware.
non-volatile: Keeps its contents when the power is off.
packet: A small chunk of data sent across a network.
parameter: A value passed into a subprogram.
penetration testing: Authorised testers deliberately trying to break in to find weaknesses.
peripheral: A device connected to a computer, such as a keyboard or printer.
phishing: Tricking people into giving up information, often with fake emails.
pixel: One tiny dot of colour in an image.
primary key: A field that uniquely identifies each row in a table.
procedure: A subprogram that does an action without necessarily returning a value.
protocol: An agreed set of rules for communication.
pseudocode: Structured, plain-English-like text that expresses logic without being a real language.
register: Tiny, very fast storage inside the CPU.
resolution: The number of pixels in an image.
router: A device that forwards data between networks.
sample rate: How many samples of a sound are taken per second.
sequence: Running statements one after another in order.
social engineering: Tricking people into giving up information or access.
SQL injection: Inserting malicious code into a database query through an input field.
switch: A device that connects devices in a network and passes data to the right one.
topology: The way the devices on a network are arranged.
trademark: Legal protection for brand names and logos.
translator: Software that converts a program into machine code.
trace table: A table that records variable values at each step of an algorithm.
Unicode: A character set that can represent characters from every written language.
validation: Checking input is sensible before it's used. It doesn't prove it's correct.
volatile: Loses its contents when the power is off.
binary: Base 2: numbers written with only 0s and 1s.
linear search: Checks each item in a list one at a time until it finds the target.
binary search: Repeatedly halves a sorted list, keeping the half that could hold the target.
bubble sort: Repeatedly swaps neighbouring items that are in the wrong order.
merge sort: Splits the list in half again and again, then merges the sorted parts back together.
Boolean: A data type with only two values: True or False.
modulus: The remainder after a division, e.g. 7 MOD 2 = 1.
defragmentation: Rearranging the pieces of files on a disk so they can be read faster.
bit: The smallest unit of data: a single 0 or 1.
flowchart: A diagram that shows the steps of an algorithm using standard shapes.
debugger: A tool for stepping through code and checking variable values as it runs.
ransomware: Malware that locks your files until you pay.
vulnerability: A weakness that an attacker could exploit.
